title: Jeremiah 49:1–6
context: The LORD speaks through Jeremiah concerning the children of Ammon, Israel’s neighbor east of the Jordan. He asks why Malcam possesses the territory of Gad, as though Israel had no heir. Malcam is commonly taken as the name of the Ammonite god also called Milcom (compare 1 Kings 11:5; Zephaniah 1:5), though some translations and interpreters read the same letters as their king; verse 3, where Malcam goes into captivity with his priests and princes, fits either sense (compare Amos 1:15). The LORD announces war against Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, commonly located at modern Amman, and calls Heshbon and the daughters of Rabbah to lament; the Ai named here is not the town of Joshua’s day, and its location is uncertain. Ammon is rebuked for trusting in its valleys and treasures, and the LORD says he will drive its people out. The unit ends with a promise: afterward the LORD will reverse the captivity of the children of Ammon, a word that stands alongside similar promises to Egypt and Moab (46:26; 48:47) and to Elam (49:39). Compare the oracles against Ammon in Amos 1:13–15 and Ezekiel 25:1–7. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as shared ground about God’s justice over the nations and his mercy beyond judgment.

verses.text: Of the children of Ammon. The LORD says: “Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then does Malcam possess Gad, and his people dwell in its cities?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking why Malcam possesses Gad, as though Israel had no heir. God defends the inheritance he gave his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the true owner of the land, rebuking Ammon’s seizure of Israel’s territory. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical frame.

verses.text: Therefore behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will cause an alarm of war to be heard against Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and it will become a desolate heap, and her daughters will be burned with fire; then Israel will possess those who possessed him,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD announcing war against Rabbah and saying Israel will possess those who possessed him. Wrongs will be reversed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God promising to vindicate Israel against its neighbor. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, within the history of Israel and Ammon (compare Amos 1:14).

verses.text: “Wail, Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste! Cry, you daughters of Rabbah! Clothe yourself in sackcloth. Lament, and run back and forth among the fences; for Malcam will go into captivity, his priests and his princes together.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Heshbon and the daughters of Rabbah called to wail because Malcam goes into captivity with his priests and princes. Their trust proves empty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fall of Ammon’s god or king as exposing false confidence. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober lament over coming loss.

verses.text: Why do you boast in the valleys, your flowing valley, backsliding daughter? You trusted in her treasures, saying, ‘Who will come to me?’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ammon rebuked for boasting in its fertile valleys and trusting its treasures. Wealth breeds a false sense of safety.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see pride in resources condemned (compare Jeremiah 48:29). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against trusting riches rather than God.

verses.text: Behold, I will bring a terror on you,” says the Lord, GOD of Armies, “from all who are around you. All of you will be driven completely out, and there will be no one to gather together the fugitives.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lord GOD of Armies saying he will bring terror from all around and drive Ammon out with no one to gather the fugitives. The judgment is thorough.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign power over the nations. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, in its historical setting.

verses.text: “But afterward I will reverse the captivity of the children of Ammon,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD promising that afterward he will reverse the captivity of Ammon. God’s mercy extends even to Israel’s neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same promise as a sign of God’s kindness to the nations (compare Jeremiah 48:47; 46:26). Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s mercy beyond judgment.
